title: Light-industrial / warehouse temporary staffing (Chicago-area, DTLSA-regulated)
subindustry: Temporary help — light industrial, warehouse, food production
product_service: W-2 temporary workers (pickers/packers, machine operators, assemblers, forklift operators, sanitation) supplied to client sites at an hourly bill rate; agency is employer of record and handles recruiting, payroll, taxes, workers' comp and DTLSA compliance.
target_customer: Plant, warehouse and HR managers at 50–1,000-employee manufacturers, 3PLs and food processors in Cook, DuPage, Will, Kane and Lake counties.
purchase_motivation: Variable/peak demand, absenteeism coverage, outsourcing high-turnover hourly recruiting, try-before-hire.
spending_evidence: US staffing firms employed ~2.0M temp/contract workers per week in Q4 2025 [C, WS12-S013]; SIA forecasts US industrial staffing revenue +7% in 2026 [C, WS12-S014]; the DTLSA amendments target >650,000 temporary workers in Illinois [A, WS12-S001]; PeopleReady (TrueBlue) alone billed $883.9M in 2025 [B, WS12-S010].
representative_operators: TrueBlue/PeopleReady — 2025 segment revenue $883.9M, segment profit $6.5M (~0.7%) [B, WS12-S010]
Hundreds of independent Chicago-area agencies on IDOL's 2026 registered-agency list [A, WS12-S004]
revenue_mechanism: Hourly bill rate = pay rate × markup covering FICA, FUTA/SUTA, workers' comp, DTLSA compliance cost and margin; billed weekly for hours worked; occasional conversion fees.
typical_transaction_value: Per worker roughly $21–26/hr billed on ~$16–18/hr pay → ~$40–50k annual billing per full-time temp [E]; a typical small client uses 5–40 temps.
direct_costs: Wages; employer FICA 7.65%; FUTA/IL SUTA; workers' comp (industrial classes — Illinois rates MISSING); compensable DTLSA safety training; equal-pay uplift after 720 hrs; benefits cash-equivalent after 720 hrs; transportation if provided.
contribution_profit_note: Incumbent gross margin 22.8% and SG&A 23.0% of revenue at TrueBlue → ~0.7% adjusted EBITDA [B, WS12-S010]. New entrant est. ~$3–5 gross profit per worker-hour → ~$6–10k GP per full-time temp-year; ~80–120 temps on billing needed to cover a minimal branch [E].
working_capital_note: Weekly payroll vs. client net-30 to net-60 → 5–9 weeks of payroll float; factoring advances 75–95% at ~1–5% of invoice [D, WS12-S016, WS12-S017]; WC carriers may demand deposits; payroll-tax trust-fund liability is personal risk.
sales_cycle: 2–8 weeks for owner-managed plants; larger sites buy via MSP/VMS with vendor qualification.
repeat_purchase: recurring-contract — weekly billing on open orders, but very high worker churn (2025 industry turnover 376%) [C, WS12-S013]
acquisition_channels: Job boards and community recruiting for worker supply
customer_accessibility: Buyers are identifiable and reachable, but most already run 2–5 agencies; displacing an incumbent requires better fill rates on hard shifts.
supplier_accessibility: Labor supply is the real supply chain: continuous recruiting needed; confirmed available but costly to retain [E].
competitive_intensity: extreme — national incumbents earn <1% EBITDA and hundreds of local agencies compete on price.
entry_strategy: Niche fill (2nd/3rd shift, food-grade sanitation, bilingual crews) with on-site coordinator and DTLSA-clean compliance as a selling point to risk-averse clients now jointly exposed under the Act.
licenses: IDOL DTLSA registration before operating: annual fee $3,000 per agency + $750 per branch, surety bond, client re-verification Mar 1/Sep 1 [A, WS12-S004]; equal pay after >720 hours at the same client in 12 months (PA 103-1030; clock from Apr 1, 2024) [C, WS12-S003]; equal benefits or hourly cash equivalent after >720 hours — preliminary injunction DENIED May 22, 2025, so enforceable [A, WS12-S001]; annual per-client general safety training at agency cost, compensable time [A, WS12-S006]; Section 67 'interested party' suits held unconstitutional by Cook County circuit court (Mar & May 2026), on appeal; IDOL not issuing right-to-sue notices meanwhile [A, WS12-S004; C, WS12-S005]. Plus IL Dept. of Employment Security UI account, workers' comp policy (IL rates for industrial classes MISSING).
regulatory_barriers: Illinois is the most demanding state for this segment: equal pay/benefits calculations depend on client data; joint client liability; record-keeping and notice duties; litigation history 2023–2026 [A, WS12-S001; A, WS12-S004].
operational_risks: Workplace injuries and WC claims; no-shows; DTLSA notice/training errors; client concentration; on-site safety failures attributed to agency.
financial_risks: Thin margin plus WC loss development can wipe out a year's profit; bad debt; payroll tax liabilities; dependence on factoring.
geographic_constraints: Branch radius ~20–30 miles; Illinois law applies to Illinois placements.
founder_expertise: Payroll tax, workers' comp risk management, DTLSA compliance, labor recruiting (Spanish strongly helpful).
staffing: Recruiter/dispatcher from day 1; on-site coordinator per large client; payroll/compliance admin by ~50 temps.
automation_potential: Shift-confirmation apps, AI applicant screening, scheduling and timekeeping reduce coordinator time; recruiting, retention, safety and client relationships remain human. AI substitution risk to demand: low near term (robotics slow), but software lowers barriers for app-based competitors.
delegation_potential: Branch-manager model is standard in the industry; delegable after ~2 years.
scalability: Branch replication possible but each branch needs WC collateral and payroll float; returns thin.
expansion: On-site managed programs, payrolling, skilled trades (WS12-002).
roic_note: Capital tied up in payroll float and WC collateral (~$60–150k at $2–3M revenue) [E]; at 2–5% operating margin ROIC is modest and volatile.
critical_assumptions: New entrant can price at 30–40% markup despite incumbents
WC premiums for warehouse/factory classes in IL are affordable for a new policy
Clients supply comparator wage/benefit data needed for 720-hour compliance
unanswered_questions: Illinois workers' comp loss costs/rates for classes 8292, 3632, 2003 etc. for a new staffing account
Has the Seventh Circuit or Illinois Supreme Court ruled further on DTLSA §42/§67 since May 2026?
How have Chicago-area clients changed temp usage (assignment caps at 720 hrs) since April 2024?
Initial (vs renewal) DTLSA registration fee and bond amount
failure_modes: Large WC claim or experience-mod spike
Client non-payment while payroll keeps running
DTLSA wage/benefit miscalculation leading to back-pay claims
Losing anchor client to a cheaper agency
score_rationale: fcf/roic 3: incumbent adj. EBITDA 0.7% [B] and float-heavy model. entry 2: commodity with entrenched scale players. cash 2: weekly payroll vs net-30/60. feasibility 5: no professional license but heaviest state compliance regime in the US for this segment. resilience 3: highly cyclical (first labor cut in recessions).
preliminary_verdict: reject — thin, cyclical margins with payroll float, WC risk and Illinois DTLSA equal-pay/benefit and litigation exposure; incumbents earn <1% EBITDA.

title: Skilled-trades & industrial maintenance contract staffing for manufacturers
subindustry: Skilled industrial contract staffing (maintenance mechanics, industrial electricians, welders, CNC machinists)
product_service: W-2 contract skilled tradespeople placed on multi-week to multi-month assignments (shutdowns, backlog, vacancies) plus temp-to-hire conversions.
target_customer: Maintenance/plant managers at 100–2,000-employee Midwest manufacturers, food plants and distribution centers.
purchase_motivation: Chronic skilled-labor shortage, downtime cost of unfilled maintenance roles, planned shutdowns.
spending_evidence: SIA raised 2026 US industrial staffing growth forecast to 7% [C, WS12-S014]; segment-specific Illinois spend MISSING.
representative_operators: National skilled-trades staffing divisions exist (e.g., trade-focused units of large staffing groups) — specific revenues not verified [E]
revenue_mechanism: Hourly bill rate on pay rate (markup ~35–55% [E]); per diem/travel pass-through for traveling techs; conversion fees.
typical_transaction_value: ~$45–70/hr billed on ~$30–45/hr pay [E]; a 3-month assignment ≈ $25–35k billing.
direct_costs: Wages, payroll taxes, workers' comp (higher-hazard trade classes — IL rates MISSING), tools/PPE, travel per diem, DTLSA training and 720-hour equal pay uplift.
contribution_profit_note: ~$10–18 GP per hour → ~$18–30k GP per full-time contractor-year [E]; 15 contractors on billing ≈ $300–450k GP [E].
working_capital_note: Weekly payroll vs net-30/45 → ~$8–12k float per contractor [E]; factoring available at ~1–5% of invoice [D, WS12-S017].
sales_cycle: Weeks for urgent vacancies at owner-managed plants; months for vendor approval at large manufacturers.
repeat_purchase: recurring-contract — repeat orders from satisfied plants; assignments 1–9 months [E]
acquisition_channels: Trade-school and union-adjacent networks for supply
customer_accessibility: Plants identifiable from public data; buyers responsive when a qualified tech is in hand (candidate-led selling).
supplier_accessibility: Qualified techs scarce and courted by many recruiters; supply is the binding constraint [E].
competitive_intensity: high — many agencies, but few with deep skilled benches.
entry_strategy: Candidate-first: build a vetted bench of 20–40 maintenance techs/electricians with skills testing; sell 'tech available Monday' to plants with open roles.
licenses: DTLSA registration likely applies (non-clerical/professional labor) — $3,000/yr + $750/branch, bond [A, WS12-S004]; 720-hour equal pay and benefits rules [A, WS12-S001; C, WS12-S003]; trade licensing (e.g., municipal electrician licenses) may apply to some tasks — unverified [E].
regulatory_barriers: Same DTLSA regime as WS12-001; longer assignments hit the 720-hour equal pay/benefit trigger more often.
operational_risks: Injury exposure, skills mismatches, poaching of techs by clients without conversion fees.
financial_risks: WC claims; payroll float; downturn in manufacturing capex.
geographic_constraints: Regional; traveling-tech model can serve the Midwest.
founder_expertise: Understanding industrial maintenance skills and testing; manufacturing relationships.
staffing: Technical recruiter with trades background early; account manager by year 2.
automation_potential: AI sourcing, skills-assessment scheduling, credential tracking; physical trade work has low AI substitution risk.
delegation_potential: Recruiter/account-manager roles standard; delegable in 2–3 years.
scalability: Regional to multi-state via traveling techs; reinvestment mainly working capital.
expansion: Direct-hire fees for same trades (WS12-014), shutdown crews, apprenticeship pipelines.
roic_note: Float ~$150–250k at 20 contractors [E]; 15–30% operating-profit-to-capital plausible, better if C2C/1099 crews (misclassification risk).
critical_assumptions: Markup of 35–55% achievable on scarce trades
Bench of qualified techs can be built without trade background
WC cost for trade classes manageable
unanswered_questions: IL workers' comp rates for millwright/electrician/welder classes in staffing
Whether DTLSA's definition covers skilled trades in all cases
Typical conversion-fee terms in Chicago manufacturing
score_rationale: Better spread and lower AI risk than general labor, but still DTLSA-covered, float-heavy and supply-constrained; economics are E-level estimates.
preliminary_verdict: hold — wider spreads than general labor but candidate supply, WC and Illinois DTLSA costs blunt returns; worth comparing with direct-hire trades recruiting.

title: CDL driver staffing / driver leasing to private fleets and shippers
subindustry: Driver staffing (Class A/B CDL, non-CDL delivery)
product_service: Qualified CDL drivers supplied on temporary or dedicated lease to private fleets (distributors, manufacturers, municipalities) with DQ files, drug/alcohol testing program and payroll handled by agency.
target_customer: Transportation/fleet managers at private-fleet operators (food distribution, building materials, waste haulers) in the Chicago region.
purchase_motivation: Driver shortage/absences, seasonal peaks, offloading DOT compliance paperwork.
spending_evidence: MISSING for driver-staffing spend specifically; general industrial staffing growth +7% 2026 [C, WS12-S014].
representative_operators: National driver-staffing operators exist (e.g., divisions of large staffing groups) — not verified this session [E]
revenue_mechanism: Hourly bill rate over driver pay; or weekly lease fee per dedicated driver.
direct_costs: Driver wages, payroll taxes, workers' comp (driver classes are high-rated — IL rates MISSING), drug/alcohol testing, MVR/background checks, possible non-owned/hired auto or contingent liability coverage.
working_capital_note: Weekly payroll vs net-30/45; insurance deposits; factoring common.
sales_cycle: 1–3 months; safety-department vetting of the agency's compliance program.
acquisition_channels: Driver recruiting via CDL schools and job boards
customer_accessibility: Fleets identifiable via FMCSA registration data; buyers cautious because driver accidents create nuclear-verdict liability.
supplier_accessibility: Drivers with clean MVRs scarce and in demand [E].
entry_strategy: Tight compliance package (DQ files, testing, MVR monitoring) for small private fleets without safety departments.
licenses: DTLSA registration likely ($3,000/yr + $750/branch + bond) [A, WS12-S004]; FMCSA driver qualification and drug/alcohol testing obligations under 49 CFR Parts 382/391 (not fetched this session) [E].
regulatory_barriers: Shared DOT compliance responsibility; auto-liability allocation contracts; IL equal-pay rules on long assignments [C, WS12-S003].
operational_risks: Serious crash involving a placed driver; failed drug tests; driver no-shows.
financial_risks: Liability claims beyond insurance; WC; payroll float.
automation_potential: Compliance tracking software (DQ files, license expiry); demand-side substitution by autonomous trucks is long-dated but real for long-haul.
scalability: Regional branches; insurance capacity limits growth.
roic_note: Float + insurance collateral against 3–6% operating margin; tail-risk liability dominates.
critical_assumptions: Insurers will cover a new driver-staffing agency at affordable rates
Clients retain auto liability contractually
unanswered_questions: Cost and availability of contingent auto liability for new driver-leasing firms in IL
IL WC rates for driver classes (7228/7229/7219)
score_rationale: Low margin, high liability tail and insurance dependence; feasibility 4 because insurance/DOT compliance structuring is hard for a new entrant.
preliminary_verdict: reject — thin margins with catastrophic liability tail and insurance gatekeeping; not suited to a first business.

title: Office/admin and accounting-finance contract staffing (clerical/professional, DTLSA-exempt)
subindustry: Office/clerical and accounting & finance temporary/contract staffing
product_service: Contract AP/AR clerks, staff accountants, payroll specialists, admin assistants and customer-service reps on hourly assignments, plus temp-to-hire.
target_customer: Controllers, CFOs and office managers at 20–500-employee Chicago-area companies, nonprofits and professional firms.
purchase_motivation: Month-end/close backlogs, leave coverage, system conversions, vacancy coverage.
spending_evidence: Robert Half contract talent revenue $2.99B in 2025 at 39.0% gross margin [B, WS12-S007]; Kforce FA revenue $98.7M, down 12.3% in 2025 [A, WS12-S009].
representative_operators: Robert Half — contract talent GM 39.0% but segment operating margin -0.8% in 2025 [B, WS12-S007]
Kforce FA — avg bill rate ~$53/hr Q4 2025 [A, WS12-S009]
revenue_mechanism: Hourly bill rate on pay rate; conversion fees on temp-to-hire.
typical_transaction_value: ~$35–60/hr billed [E, anchored to Kforce FA ~$53/hr A]; a 3-month assignment ≈ $18–30k billing.
direct_costs: Wages, payroll taxes, low-hazard clerical workers' comp, benefits under ACA thresholds.
contribution_profit_note: ~$10–16 GP/hr → ~$18–30k GP per full-time contractor-year [E]; incumbent RH shows SG&A (recruiter pay, branches) consumes nearly all GP at cycle trough [B, WS12-S007].
working_capital_note: Payroll weekly/biweekly vs net-30; ~$6–10k float per contractor [E]; factoring 1–5% [D, WS12-S017].
repeat_purchase: recurring-contract — repeat orders from same controllers
customer_accessibility: Reachable via standard B2B outreach; incumbents' brands strong.
supplier_accessibility: Clerical candidates plentiful; quality accounting talent tighter [E].
competitive_intensity: high — Robert Half, Accountemps legacy, many boutiques.
entry_strategy: Narrow specialization (e.g., ERP-specific accounting contractors such as NetSuite/Sage Intacct close support) with technically vetted talent.
licenses: IDOL indicates agencies placing only clerical/professional workers may be exempt from DTLSA registration (56 IAC 260) [A, WS12-S004]; if doing direct-hire, IL Private Employment Agency license ($250–500 fee, $5,000 bond) [A, WS12-S015].
regulatory_barriers: Low; standard payroll compliance and IL wage laws.
operational_risks: Contractor quality; client poaching without fees.
financial_risks: Demand contraction: RH and Kforce FA revenues fell in 2025 [A, WS12-S009; B, WS12-S007].
geographic_constraints: Mostly local/hybrid; remote assignments widen reach.
founder_expertise: Must learn accounting roles/ERP skill vetting.
staffing: Recruiter with accounting background by month 6; account managers later.
automation_potential: AI improves matching and admin; but AI/automation directly substitutes for AP/AR/data-entry and admin work — Robert Half's 10-K lists AI substitution as a risk [A, WS12-S008]. Net: high demand-side substitution risk.
scalability: Moderate; local ceiling unless specialized nationally (remote).
expansion: Direct-hire accounting recruiting; fractional controller services (cross-stream WS02).
roic_note: Float modest (~$100–200k at 20 contractors) [E]; ROIC moderate.
critical_assumptions: SMBs will use a new boutique over RH
AI does not shrink entry-level finance/admin temp demand faster than the firm grows
unanswered_questions: Exact 56 IAC 260 exemption scope for clerical/professional agencies
Local bill rates for AP/AR clerks in Chicago 2026
failure_modes: Secular decline in clerical temp demand from automation
score_rationale: feasibility 8: likely DTLSA-exempt. resilience 3: cyclical plus visible AI substitution (FA -12.3% at Kforce). entry 3: crowded with strong brands.
preliminary_verdict: hold — avoids DTLSA but faces the clearest AI substitution headwind in staffing; viable only as a narrow ERP/finance-tech specialty.

title: IT contract staffing for mid-market companies
product_service: Contract software engineers, data/BI analysts, cloud/DevOps, ERP and infrastructure specialists on 3–12-month assignments, plus conversions.
target_customer: CIOs, IT directors and engineering managers at 200–5,000-employee Midwest companies not locked into MSP/VMS programs.
purchase_motivation: Project capacity without headcount, specialized skills for migrations, budget flexibility.
spending_evidence: Kforce Technology revenue $1.2B in 2025 (-4.8%) [A, WS12-S009]; SIA March 2026 forecast IT staffing growth ~1% [C, WS12-S014].
representative_operators: Kforce — Flex GM 25.8%, operating margin 3.8%, Tech avg bill rate ~$89/hr, avg assignment 10 months (2025) [A, WS12-S009]
Robert Half technology contract practice within contract talent (GM 39.0% blended) [B, WS12-S007]
revenue_mechanism: Hourly bill rate; spread over consultant pay (W-2) or over subcontractor rate (C2C); conversion fees.
typical_transaction_value: ~$75–110/hr billed [E, anchored to Kforce ~$89/hr A]; 10-month assignment ≈ $120–170k billing.
direct_costs: Consultant wages and payroll taxes (or C2C subcontractor invoices), benefits, low clerical WC.
contribution_profit_note: At $85/hr × ~1,850 billable hrs × 22% GM ≈ $35k GP per consultant-year [E]; 12 consultants ≈ $415k GP, ~ $200–250k operating profit after a lean team [E].
working_capital_note: Biweekly payroll vs net-30 to net-60 (large clients push 60+) → ~$15–20k float per W-2 consultant [E]; factoring at ~1–5% of invoice would consume ~5–20% of GP [D, WS12-S016, WS12-S017].
sales_cycle: 1–3 months to first requisition; vendor onboarding at mid-market firms.
customer_accessibility: Mid-market reachable via standard B2B outreach; enterprises gated by MSP/VMS and preferred-vendor lists [E].
supplier_accessibility: Contractor supply plentiful after 2023–2025 tech layoffs; quality vetting is the differentiator [E].
competitive_intensity: extreme — thousands of IT staffing firms including offshore-led bench sellers.
entry_strategy: Founder's technical background as vetting wedge; narrow stack specialization; responsive senior-only bench.
licenses: Professional IT staffing likely exempt from DTLSA registration (clerical/professional exemption) [A, WS12-S004]; IL Private Employment Agency license if charging placement/conversion fees — likely needed [A, WS12-S015]; immigration (H-1B) sponsorship optional and complex.
regulatory_barriers: Low; worker classification risk on C2C/1099.
operational_risks: Consultant fraud/proxy interviews (industry problem), early terminations, client concentration.
financial_risks: Float; slow-paying enterprises; demand cyclicality in IT budgets.
staffing: 1–2 technical recruiters by month 6; account manager year 2; payroll outsourced.
automation_potential: AI sourcing/screening/matching cuts recruiter time materially; but AI coding tools reduce demand for junior contract developers (RH 10-K risk factor [A, WS12-S008]); senior/architectural roles more durable.
delegation_potential: Recruiter/AM roles standard; delegable in 2–3 years.
scalability: Multi-region via remote; many firms reach $10–50M revenue (D, not verified).
expansion: Direct-hire IT, statement-of-work project delivery, nearshore teams (WS12-012).
roic_note: Capital = float (~$200–300k at 15 consultants, partly factored) [E]; operating profit/capital ~50–100% at scale.
critical_assumptions: Mid-market clients outside VMS will add a new vendor
22% GM achievable as boutique
AI does not cut contract developer demand faster than niche share gains
unanswered_questions: Share of Chicago mid-market IT spend going through MSP/VMS
Typical payment terms for mid-market IT contracts in 2026
failure_modes: Demand drops as AI coding tools spread
score_rationale: fcf 5: $35k GP per consultant scales cleanly. access 4: VMS gating. cash 3: float. entry 3: extreme competition though founder tech fit helps.
preliminary_verdict: hold — real scale path and founder fit, but float, VMS gating and AI demand erosion; compare against direct-hire IT recruiting.

title: Scientific, lab, quality & engineering contract staffing
product_service: Contract lab technicians, QC chemists, microbiologists, validation/quality engineers and manufacturing engineers for labs and regulated manufacturers; temp-to-hire and direct-hire.
target_customer: Lab managers, QA directors and engineering managers at Chicago-area food, cosmetics, chemical, med-device and contract-testing labs (mid-size, non-VMS), plus university core labs.
purchase_motivation: Regulated QC work cannot stop (FDA/USDA/ISO), project surges, validation campaigns, leave coverage.
spending_evidence: MISSING for segment size; Kforce/Robert Half data show 25.8–39% contract gross margins for professional staffing [A, WS12-S009; B, WS12-S007].
representative_operators: Large science-staffing brands operate nationally (e.g., units of Allegis, Kelly) — not verified this session [E]
revenue_mechanism: Hourly bill rate on pay rate; conversion/direct-hire fees.
direct_costs: Wages, payroll taxes, WC (lab classes moderate), benefits, background/drug screens.
working_capital_note: Weekly/biweekly payroll vs net-30/45; ~$8–15k float per contractor [E]; factoring available [D, WS12-S017].
sales_cycle: 1–3 months at mid-size labs; big pharma via MSP (long).
repeat_purchase: recurring-contract — repeat requisitions from same lab managers
acquisition_channels: University placement offices and alumni networks for supply
customer_accessibility: Mid-size labs reachable and underserved relative to pharma; buyers value technically credible recruiters [E].
supplier_accessibility: New science graduates plentiful; experienced QC/validation talent tighter [E].
competitive_intensity: moderate-high — national brands dominate large accounts; fewer boutiques in mid-market.
entry_strategy: Founder's research background as credibility wedge: technical screening (instrument, GMP, method validation) that generalist recruiters cannot do.
licenses: Professional scientific staffing may qualify for DTLSA clerical/professional exemption — lab-tech classification uncertain [A, WS12-S004]; IL Private Employment Agency license for direct-hire fees [A, WS12-S015].
regulatory_barriers: Clients' GMP/GLP training requirements; otherwise low.
operational_risks: Contractor errors in regulated labs; conversion leakage.
financial_risks: Float; biotech funding cycles (less so in food/industrial labs).
founder_expertise: Recruiting craft; GMP vocabulary (founder research background helps).
staffing: Scientific recruiter by month 6; onboarding coordinator year 2.
automation_potential: AI sourcing/screening; hands-on bench work has low AI substitution risk; lab automation slowly reduces routine tech headcount.
delegation_potential: Recruiters with science degrees hireable; delegable in 2–3 years.
scalability: Regional with multiple metros; adjacent clinical-research staffing.
expansion: Direct-hire science recruiting; lab-services outsourcing; clinical-research staffing (cross-stream WS04).
roic_note: Float ~$150–250k at 15–20 contractors [E]; ROIC ~50–100% at scale.
critical_assumptions: Enough non-VMS mid-size labs in region
Lab techs fall under DTLSA professional exemption or compliance cost is manageable
Founder credibility translates into fill wins
unanswered_questions: Count of Chicago-area mid-size labs/QC operations
Bill/pay spreads for QC chemists locally
DTLSA classification of lab technicians
score_rationale: entry 5 and resilience 6: technical vetting wedge plus regulated, hands-on work with low AI substitution; cash 3 due to float; evidence E.
preliminary_verdict: advance — best founder-fit staffing niche: technical credibility wedge, regulated demand, lower AI substitution; needs segment-size and spread evidence.

title: Multifamily property-management staffing (leasing agents, maintenance techs, porters)
product_service: Temporary and temp-to-hire leasing consultants, assistant/community managers, maintenance technicians, make-ready/turn crews and porters for apartment communities.
target_customer: Regional managers and HR at property-management companies running 500–20,000 units in the Chicago metro (and Midwest).
purchase_motivation: Vacancy coverage at individual communities, lease-up of new buildings, seasonal turn volume, high on-site turnover.
spending_evidence: BGSF property-management staffing revenue $26.9M in Q3 2025 and ~$22M in Q4 2025 [B, WS12-S011; C, WS12-S012].
representative_operators: BGSF (BG Multifamily) — Q3 2025 gross margin 35.9%, operating loss $0.9M; Q4 GM 35.0%, revenue -9.4% y/y [B, WS12-S011; C, WS12-S012]
revenue_mechanism: Hourly bill rate on pay rate; conversion fees; project pricing for turn crews.
typical_transaction_value: ~$28–45/hr billed for leasing/maintenance roles [E]; 4–8-week coverage ≈ $5–15k per assignment [E].
direct_costs: Wages, payroll taxes, workers' comp (maintenance classes higher than leasing), tools for techs, DTLSA compliance for maintenance/porter roles if covered.
contribution_profit_note: Incumbent GM ~35–36% but segment operating loss in 2025 [B, WS12-S011] — high GM, short assignments, heavy recruiting SG&A. New entrant est. ~$8–14 GP/hr [E].
working_capital_note: Weekly payroll vs net-30 from property-management companies; float moderate because assignments are short [E].
sales_cycle: Weeks with regional managers; corporate vendor approval at large REIT-managed portfolios.
repeat_purchase: recurring-contract — frequent short orders from same portfolios
acquisition_channels: Regional managers via local apartment association events
customer_accessibility: Concentrated, identifiable buyer set (management companies with public unit counts); repeat need frequent [E].
supplier_accessibility: Leasing talent from retail/hospitality pools; HVAC/EPA-certified maintenance techs scarcer [E].
competitive_intensity: moderate — few vertical specialists; general agencies weak at leasing skills.
entry_strategy: Vertical specialization with pre-trained leasing consultants (property-management software proficiency) and fast weekend coverage; density in one metro.
licenses: DTLSA registration likely required for maintenance/porter placements ($3,000/yr + $750/branch, bond) [A, WS12-S004]; 720-hour equal pay/benefits on long assignments [A, WS12-S001; C, WS12-S003]; IL Private Employment Agency license if charging direct-hire fees [A, WS12-S015]; leasing agents may need IL real-estate leasing agent licensing when acting for brokers — unverified [E].
regulatory_barriers: Possible real-estate leasing-license requirement for leasing roles (verify); DTLSA for maintenance roles.
operational_risks: Maintenance injuries; client churn when rents soften; conversion leakage.
financial_risks: Demand tied to apartment operator budgets (BGSF revenue fell 9.4% on client cost pressure) [C, WS12-S012].
automation_potential: AI leasing assistants (chat/voice) are actively substituting for leasing-agent hours — material substitution risk for the leasing half; maintenance work low AI risk.
scalability: Metro replication; ceiling set by vertical size.
roic_note: Float modest; ROIC moderate if utilization high.
critical_assumptions: 35%-type GM achievable by boutique
Leasing roles do not require a real-estate license in the staffing structure
unanswered_questions: IL real-estate leasing agent license applicability to temp leasing consultants
DTLSA coverage of property maintenance roles
Chicago multifamily operator count and temp spend
failure_modes: AI leasing agents remove leasing-temp demand
